section.title: My Heart Is Steadfast
section.sectionRationale: Written while David fled from Saul into a cave, likely at Adullam or En Gedi, 1 Samuel 22:1, 24:3. David takes refuge in the shadow of God's wings, and moves from surrounded danger to a fixed resolve to praise, framed by the refrain be exalted, O God, above the heavens, may Your glory cover all the earth, also found in Psalm 108.
section.thesis: Hiding from Saul in a cave, David takes refuge in the shadow of God's wings, and even surrounded by lions moves from fear to fixed praise, longing for God's glory to fill the whole earth, a longing answered when Christ's glory is proclaimed to every nation.
section.frameNote: Four movements: refuge in the shadow of God's wings amid danger; the surrounding lions and the enemies' own trap turned against them; the settled resolve, my heart is steadfast; and the closing refrain of praise among the nations, be exalted, O God, above the heavens.

units.label: In the shadow of Your wings

verses.text: Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy, for in You my soul takes {{chaseh|refuge}}. In the shadow of Your wings I will take shelter until the danger has passed.
I cry out to God Most High, to God who fulfills His purpose for me.
He reaches down from heaven and saves me; He rebukes those who trample me. Selah God sends forth His {{chesed|loving devotion}} and His truth.

units.label: My soul is among lions
units.note: surrounded, yet the enemies fall into their own trap

verses.text: My soul is among the lions; I lie down with ravenous beasts, with men whose teeth are spears and arrows, whose tongues are sharp swords.
Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your {{kavod|glory}} cover all the earth.
They spread a net for my feet; my soul was despondent. They dug a pit before me, but they themselves have fallen into it! Selah

units.label: My heart is steadfast, O God

verses.text: My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast. I will sing and make music.

Awake, my glory! Awake, O harp and lyre! 
I will awaken the dawn.

units.label: Be exalted, O God, above the heavens
units.note: the refrain of praise among the nations

verses.text: I will praise You, O Lord, among the nations; I will sing Your praises among the peoples.
For Your loving devotion reaches to the heavens, and Your faithfulness to the clouds.
Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your glory cover all the earth.

chaseh.gloss: To take refuge, to seek shelter. David's soul takes refuge in God as a bird shelters under a parent's wings, an image of vulnerable, trusting dependence rather than self-reliant strength, echoed in Ruth 2:12 and taken up by Jesus Himself in Matthew 23:37.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast, covenant loving devotion, appearing in verses 3 and 10, the quality of God's character David trusts to reach down and save him and to extend as high as the heavens themselves.

kavod.gloss: Glory, weight, honor. The refrain's prayer, may Your glory cover all the earth, longs for God's own weighty, visible splendor to be acknowledged by every nation, not merely for David's personal rescue.

basic.context: Hiding from Saul in a cave, David pictures himself sheltering in the shadow of God's wings like a frightened bird, even while surrounded by enemies as dangerous as lions with teeth like spears. Remarkably, the psalm's refrain is not merely a plea for personal safety but a prayer that God's glory would cover the whole earth. By the psalm's second half, David's fear has become fixed, steadfast praise, and his focus has widened from his own danger to God's fame among all nations.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm shows that genuine faith does not deny danger, David is quite literally among lions, but it does reframe the purpose of deliverance. David does not merely want to be saved; he wants God's glory to be seen by the whole earth. The move from anxious cry to settled resolve, my heart is steadfast, shows that fixed praise is often a deliberate choice made in the midst of danger, not only its eventual result.
basic.originalLanguages: David describes his soul as chasah, taking refuge, sheltering in the shadow of God's wings like a helpless bird. He trusts God's chesed, steadfast loving devotion, to reach down and save him, and prays that God's kavod, weighty glory, would cover the whole earth, not merely rescue him personally.
basic.typology: The wing-refuge image echoes the picture of God gathering His people as a bird gathers her young, taken up directly by Jesus in His lament over Jerusalem, and the prayer that God's glory cover the whole earth anticipates the Great Commission and the final filling of the earth with the knowledge of God's glory.
basic.christ: David's image of sheltering under God's wings is echoed by Jesus Himself, who laments over Jerusalem, how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, Matthew 23:37, revealing that the shelter David sought in God is offered personally by Christ. The refrain's longing, be exalted, O God, above the heavens, may Your glory cover all the earth, is set in motion by the Great Commission, Matthew 28:18-20, and will be finally and fully realized when the earth is filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, Habakkuk 2:14, at Christ's return.
basic.god: God is shown as a refuge as intimate and tender as a parent bird's wing, and as sovereign and exalted as the heavens themselves, reaching down personally to save while remaining worthy of praise among every nation on earth.
basic.crossReferences: Ruth 2:12 blesses Ruth for taking refuge under the wings of the LORD. Matthew 23:37 shows Jesus longing to gather Jerusalem as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings. Habakkuk 2:14 promises the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, the ultimate answer to this psalm's refrain.
basic.oneStory: Surrounded by danger, David shelters in the shadow of God's wings and moves from fear to steadfast praise, longing not merely for his own rescue but for God's glory to cover the whole earth. That longing is embodied by Christ, who gathers His people under His own care, and will be finally fulfilled when His glory fills the earth at His return.

context.literary:
The psalm is a diptych with a hinge. Verses 1 to 5 begin with a doubled plea for mercy and end on a refrain, 'Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your glory cover all the earth.' Verses 6 to 11 end on the very same refrain. The two halves are therefore rounded off in the same words, and the refrain in verse 5 comes at the lowest point, right after the lions, while the repeat in verse 11 comes at the highest point, after the vow of praise. The same sentence is prayed from the pit and from the dawn.

The two halves mirror each other in other ways. The first moves from refuge, verse 1, to rescue from heaven, verse 3, to the lions, verse 4. The second moves from the trap, verse 6, to the steady heart, verse 7, to public praise, verses 8 and 9. In verse 6 the trap is turned around, 'they themselves have fallen into it,' and this reversal lies at the centre of the second half. The doubled language is everywhere: 'have mercy on me, have mercy,' 'my heart is steadfast, my heart is steadfast,' and the opening address in verse 7 answering the plea of verse 1.

The Selah marks fall at verses 3 and 6. The first comes after the statement that God sends forth his loving devotion and truth, and the second after the pit is turned on the diggers. They give the reader a pause exactly where God is shown acting. The psalm is a prayer that ends in song, and the last two verses are entirely about praise and glory.
context.historical:
The heading says David composed the psalm when he fled from Saul into the cave. The Bible gives two cave episodes, the cave of Adullam, 1 Samuel 22:1, where his family and a band of men joined him, and the cave at En Gedi, 1 Samuel 24:3, where Saul came in to relieve himself and David spared his life. The psalm does not say which it is, and the description of being among lions and of spears and arrows fits either time. The heading also carries the phrase 'Do Not Destroy,' which stands above Psalms 57 to 59 and 75. It is probably a tune name or direction, and the word Miktam, shared by 16 and 56 to 60, is also of uncertain meaning.

The cave was a real refuge and a real trap. A fugitive in rock country could hide from pursuers, but a cave with a single mouth could become a place in which he was cornered. David's language of a net spread for his feet and a pit dug before him suits the shepherd-hunter's world he knew, where nets and pits caught animals.

The psalm later appears in a new form. Psalm 108:1-5 reuses verses 7 to 11 almost word for word, joined to a portion of Psalm 60. That shows that the later community sang these lines beyond their first occasion and treated them as a standing song of confidence that could be carried into a different crisis.
context.canonical:
The wings of God are a thread in the Psalter. Psalm 17:8 asks to be hidden in the shadow of his wings, Psalm 36:7 says that the children of men take refuge there, Psalm 61:4 asks to dwell in his tent and take refuge in the shelter of his wings, Psalm 63:7 sings for joy in their shadow, and Psalm 91:4 says that under his wings you will find refuge. The language goes back to Ruth 2:12, where Boaz blesses Ruth as one who has come to take refuge under the wings of the God of Israel, and to Deuteronomy 32:11, where God carries Israel like an eagle spreading its wings over its young. Some also hear a reference to the wings of the cherubim over the mercy seat, Exodus 25:20.

The refrain that God's glory may cover the earth is one of the great hopes of the Bible. Numbers 14:21 swears that the whole earth will be filled with the glory of the LORD, Isaiah 6:3 has the seraphim cry that all the earth is full of his glory, Habakkuk 2:14 says the earth will be filled with the knowledge of that glory as the waters cover the sea, and Psalm 8:1 says God has set his glory above the heavens. Psalm 57 prays what the prophets promise.

In the New Testament Jesus takes the wings image for himself in Matthew 23:37 and prays in John 12:28, 'Father, glorify Your name!' Paul quotes Psalm 18:49 in Romans 15:9 to show that praise among the Gentiles is part of God's plan, and the vow of verse 9 in this psalm to praise among the nations is of a piece with that hope.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David intends to teach that the direction of a prayer can change in the course of praying. The psalm begins by begging for mercy with the repeated plea, and it ends by begging for God's glory over the whole earth. Between these, nothing external alters: the lions are still there. What changes is where David is looking. The psalm is meant to show singers how a person in danger can lift the eyes and widen the horizon.

He also means to show the reversal of the trap. The enemies who dug a pit fell into it, verse 6, and David presents this as the ordinary way that God works. Hearers who are frightened are encouraged to see that the snare set for them can become the snare of the one who set it. Finally, the psalm means to promote public praise. David will sing 'among the nations,' and his rescue is to become a witness. The first hearers were meant to see that being saved carries an obligation to tell others who did it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes a man in a cave, in danger, who responds with trust. It gives no instruction to seek out caves or to go looking for lions. What is described as David's resolve, to sing and make music and to awaken the dawn, is the pattern of a person who chooses worship as an act of the will.

The psalm prescribes what it does when it teaches us a way to pray: ask for mercy, take refuge, name the danger, and lift the eyes to God's glory. The claim that the trap will turn on the trappers is a description of what happened and a settled conviction about how God works, and it is not a prediction for every case. Scripture tells us that the righteous also suffer and die, and this psalm does not contradict it. It offers confidence in God's purpose for us, verse 2, and not a promise of a particular outcome.

debates.question: Which cave is meant in the heading?

views.label: The cave of Adullam
views.case: First Samuel 22:1 says David took refuge in the cave of Adullam after leaving Gath, and his family and a crowd of distressed men gathered to him there. The mood of a man in flight and among men in need of rescue fits the psalm's plea.

views.label: The cave at En Gedi
views.case: First Samuel 24:3 has David hiding in the recesses of a cave when Saul came in, and David spared his life. The psalm's sense of Saul close at hand, of a net and a pit, and of a God who sends help from heaven suits an episode in which Saul walked into David's hiding place.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle it, and the psalm's lesson is unaffected. The story it tells is the same either way: a man in a cave who chooses to praise.

debates.question: What is 'my glory' in verse 8, which is told to awake?

views.label: David's own soul or inner being
views.case: The word for glory is used in parallel with the soul and the heart elsewhere. The BSB itself renders the same term 'tongue' in Psalm 16:9 and 'heart' in Psalm 30:12, so 'my glory' could be the noblest part of the person, the part that praises.

views.label: God's glory, called to awake
views.case: The refrain speaks of God's glory in verses 5 and 11, so the word in verse 8 might be read as that same glory. The call would then be to the glory of God to show itself, with the harp and lyre joining the cry.

debates.bearing: The first reading fits the parallel with harp and lyre, which are instruments of the praiser, and the second fits the psalm's theme. Either way David is rousing something to sing before dawn.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm's very first words carry a rhythm that English can only copy by repeating them: 'Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy.' The doubled verb is an intensifier, the cry of someone who cannot wait for the sentence to end. The verb is the language of asking for favour from one who owes nothing, and the same verb family is used in Psalm 56:1, so that the two psalms begin with one prayer. The next clause, 'until the danger has passed,' turns on a plural noun whose basic sense is ruin or calamity. It is the same plural noun that Psalm 52:2 uses of the tongue that 'devises destruction,' so the ruin David waits out is of the kind that Doeg planned. The shadow of God's wings is where the ruin can go past.

Verse 2 says God 'fulfills His purpose for me.' The Hebrew verb is one of completing, bringing something to its end. It is used in Psalm 138:8, 'The LORD will fulfill His purpose for me,' and the pairing shows that David rests not just in rescue but in a purpose that God is carrying through. The title for God here, God Most High, Elyon, is the name that stresses rule over all; in a cave, David appeals to the one who is above everything that threatens him.

Verse 3 gives two personified gifts: God 'sends forth His loving devotion and His truth.' These are the two great covenant qualities, often paired, as in Genesis 24:27, where Abraham's servant blesses the LORD who has not withheld his kindness and faithfulness. The verb 'sends forth' gives them movement, as though they set out from heaven to reach David. The same pair appears in verse 10 in a larger form, reaching to the heavens and the clouds, and this ties the two halves together.

Verse 7's 'steadfast' is a verb of establishing, being fixed in place. It is used of a heart in Psalm 112:7, 'his heart is steadfast, trusting in the LORD,' and its negative in Psalm 78:37, where the hearts of the people were not steadfast. The verb is about a person being set on a foundation and not wavering, and it makes the repetition in verse 7 sound like a settled person taking stock.

In verse 8, David says 'I will awaken the dawn,' and the ordinary expectation would be that the dawn wakes the singer. The phrasing pictures a worshipper so ready to praise that he rises before the sun. The word rendered 'glory' in the same verse, 'my glory,' is a close cousin of the word of the refrain, but it refers to David's own worth or soul and, as Psalm 16:9 and Psalm 30:12 show, is often translated as tongue or heart.

typology.type: Sheltering under the wings of God
typology.fulfillment: The image of a bird covering its young, which Psalm 57:1 uses for David in the cave, is used by Jesus of himself in Matthew 23:37, where he longs to gather Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers her chicks. The escalation is that the shelter David asked of God is now offered in the person of Christ, who gives rest to all who are weary, Matthew 11:28. The type falls short because the wings of the psalm are a figure of speech about God's protection, while in Jesus the one who protects takes on human form. It also falls short in a warning: the text says Jerusalem was not willing, and the refuge can be refused.

typology.type: The pit dug for the righteous that swallows the digger
typology.fulfillment: Verse 6's reversal, enemies falling into their own pit, repeats a pattern seen in Psalm 7:15 and Psalm 9:15. It finds its greatest instance at the cross. The rulers who laid the trap for Jesus accomplished what God had planned, Acts 2:23, and the death they devised became the defeat of death, Hebrews 2:14-15. First Corinthians 2:8 says that if the rulers had understood, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. The type falls short because the trap in the psalm falls on the enemies themselves, while at the cross the trap is turned into rescue for the very people who set it, Luke 23:34.

David's refrain, 'may Your glory cover all the earth,' is the prayer that Jesus takes into his own mouth in John 12:28, when he asks the Father to glorify his name and a voice from heaven answers that he has glorified it and will again. Paul says that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus is Lord, to the glory of God the Father, Philippians 2:9-11. The escalation is that the glory David asked for is shown in a person, John 1:14. The type falls short because the prayer is still unanswered in full, and the filling of the earth, Habakkuk 2:14, awaits the last day.

David vows to praise God among the nations and peoples, which was a remarkable wish for a man in a cave at odds with his own king. The commission Jesus gives in Matthew 28:19-20 makes the vow the church's vocation, and Romans 15:9-11 cites the same hope of Gentile praise from the Psalms. The vision of Revelation 5:9 shows a new song sung by people from every tribe and tongue and people and nation. The type falls short in that David's praise was the voice of one man, while the praise of the nations is the work of a redeemed multitude.

study.christ:
The psalm does not foretell Christ in a direct way, and it would be a mistake to treat the cave as a tomb or Saul as a code for Rome. What it does is show a pattern that Christ fulfils with greater weight. The rightful king is pursued, takes refuge in God, and sings before the rescue comes. The first Christians saw this pattern in Jesus, as they saw it in other psalms of David's suffering.

Start with the wings. In Matthew 23:37 Jesus says he has longed to gather Jerusalem's children 'as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings,' and in that sentence he takes onto himself the work the psalm gives to God. What David asked of God, Jesus says he has offered and been refused. The psalm's refuge is then not only a general comfort but a personal invitation, given by the one who will be handed over to enemies in that very city.

Next, the pit. The rulers who plotted to kill Jesus did it in the belief that they were ending a threat, and the apostles later say that they did what God's power and will had decided beforehand, Acts 4:27-28. The pit they dug became the place of their own undoing, since the death they arranged was the moment of the victory of the one they killed, Colossians 2:15. The psalm's confidence in reversal is confirmed in the resurrection.

The psalm's centre of gravity is the glory of God over all the earth. Jesus prays this in John 12:28 when he faces the hour of his death, and he says that the Father's glory is shown in his being lifted up. In John 17:1-5 he prays that the Father may glorify the Son so that the Son may glorify the Father. The prayer of Psalm 57 is therefore answered in the cross and the resurrection, and its last word is taken up in Philippians 2:9-11.

Lastly, the psalm's movement from fear to praise is a pattern for the church. Paul and Silas sang hymns in prison at midnight, Acts 16:25, and the prisoners listened. That is the psalm lived out: a steadfast heart, a song in the dark, a witness to those who overhear. The resurrection of Christ is the reason that such singing is not a pretence. We should not read too much into details, but we may say that what David chose in the cave, Christ accomplished for all who take refuge in him.
study.god:
The God of Psalm 57 is close enough to be a shelter and high enough to be exalted above the heavens. The psalm keeps both truths in the same breath. He 'reaches down from heaven and saves me,' verse 3, and he is asked to be exalted above the heavens, verse 5. David does not have to choose between a God who is near and a God who is great. The wings belong to the one whose glory covers the earth.

He is a God of purpose. The phrase 'who fulfills His purpose for me' shows that what happens to David is not random. Even in a cave, God is bringing something to completion. This is not a promise of comfort, since the lions are still there, but of meaning. The psalm shows that God's purpose is carried through in the middle of danger and not merely after it.

He is a God who sends out his covenant character. The loving devotion and truth of verse 3 and again of verse 10 are not abstractions. They go out from heaven to a man in a cave, and they reach as high as the clouds. God's faithfulness is pictured in both directions, coming down to David and stretching up past the sky. The one who is exalted above the heavens is not remote from those in need.

He is also a God who turns traps. The enemies dug a pit and fell into it. The psalm does not call David to arrange this, and it says it simply happened. That is how the Bible often speaks of justice: God lets the wicked be caught by their own devices, as in Psalm 7:15 and Psalm 9:15.

For worship, the psalm presents praise as something we may do in advance of rescue and in the company of the nations. The instruction in verses 7 and 8 shows that a heart fixed on God can wake the dawn. It also shows that the ultimate goal of a rescued life is not safety but the fame of God: what David wants most is that God's glory cover the whole earth, and he asks for his own rescue as a path to that end.

crossReferences.note: After Gath, David took refuge in the cave of Adullam, and his family and other men in distress came to him. It is one of the two caves the heading might mean, and it shows the cave as a place where a fugitive became a leader.
Saul went into a cave to relieve himself, and David and his men were hiding deep inside it. It is the other possible setting, and it shows how close the danger of verse 4 might have been.

These verses repeat Psalm 57:7-11 almost word for word. They show that David's song of steadfast praise became a standing liturgy that the community could use again whenever circumstances changed, carrying the same confidence into a new crisis.

He will cover you with his feathers and under his wings you will find refuge, and his faithfulness is a shield. It is the closest statement of the wings image and joins refuge to faithfulness as Psalm 57 does.
Boaz blesses Ruth as one who has taken refuge under the wings of the God of Israel. It shows that the image was older than David, and that a foreigner could come under the wings.
He has dug a pit and fallen into the pit of his own making. It states the same reversal as Psalm 57:6 and shows it as a regular, recurring pattern of God's justice toward the violent.
The steadfast heart that trusts in the LORD does not fear bad news. It uses the same word for a steady heart as Psalm 57:7 and explains the source of the steadiness.
The earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea. It is the prophetic counterpart of the psalm's refrain and states the goal the psalm prays for.
Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but they were unwilling. He makes the psalm's image personal and shows that the shelter of God can be refused.

Paul and Silas prayed and sang hymns in prison at midnight while the other prisoners listened. It is the psalm's steadfast heart in practice, with a song in the dark and a witness to those who overhear.

God exalted Jesus and gave him the name above all names, so that every knee bows and every tongue confesses that he is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. It is the New Testament answer to 'be exalted, O God.'

study.oneStory:
The psalm takes up a question that begins at the start of the Bible: what is the earth for? Genesis 1 describes a world that is very good and filled with creatures made to reflect God's rule, and human beings are made in his image to live in his presence. After the fall, the world is marked by violence and traps, and Psalm 57 is set in that world, a cave, lions and spears. Yet the psalm keeps the first purpose in view. It asks that God's glory cover the earth, which is the creation's original destiny.

What the psalm sets up is the great hope of the prophets and the apostles. The hope that God's glory will fill the earth is sworn in Numbers 14:21, proclaimed by the seraphim in Isaiah 6:3, and promised in Habakkuk 2:14. The prayer for a people of praise among the nations leads to the promise to Abraham that in him all nations will be blessed, Genesis 12:3, and to the commission in Matthew 28:19-20.

The story's centre is the one who took refuge in the Father in the worst place and whose glory was revealed in his being lifted up. Jesus prays the psalm's refrain in his own words and, by his death and resurrection, answers it, John 12:28, Philippians 2:9-11. Those who take refuge in him are sheltered under wings that cannot be refused once they have come, and they sing in the dark because the dawn is certain.

The end of the story is a world in which God's glory does fill the earth. Revelation 21:23 says the city has no need of sun or moon, because the glory of God gives it light, and verse 24 says the nations will walk by its light. The cave, the lions and the net are gone. The singer who vowed to praise among the nations finds the nations praising with him, and the dawn he woke is the one that does not end.

quiz.q: What historical situation is this psalm connected to?

options.text: David hiding from Saul in a cave.
options.note: The heading ties this psalm to David's flight from Saul into a cave, 1 Samuel 22:1 or 24:3.

options.text: David's victory celebration after defeating the Ammonites.
options.note: This psalm describes danger and refuge, not a victory celebration.

options.text: David's coronation in Hebron.
options.note: The psalm's setting is a cave during flight from Saul, not a coronation ceremony.

options.text: Solomon's dedication of the temple.
options.note: This is a psalm of David during his flight, not a psalm connected to Solomon's temple dedication.

quiz.q: What image does David use in verse 1 to describe his trust in God?

options.text: Taking shelter in the shadow of God's wings, like a bird sheltering under a parent.
options.note: This vivid image of vulnerable, trusting refuge opens the psalm.

options.text: Standing behind a fortified stone wall.
options.note: Fortress imagery appears in other psalms, but this specific verse uses the image of wings, not walls.

options.text: Riding into battle on a war horse.
options.note: The image used is one of shelter and vulnerability, not of military action.

options.text: Climbing to the top of a high mountain alone.
options.note: The specific image in verse 1 is refuge under wings, not a mountain ascent.

quiz.q: What surprising turn happens in verse 6 regarding David's enemies?

options.text: They dug a pit and spread a net for David, but fell into the trap they set themselves.
options.note: This is stated explicitly, a moment of poetic justice within the psalm.

options.text: They repented and became David's allies.
options.note: The text describes their own trap turning against them, not a reconciliation.

options.text: They successfully captured David.
options.note: The opposite happens; their scheme backfires and they themselves fall into the trap.

options.text: They were defeated in an open military battle.
options.note: The verse describes a trap turned against its makers, not a battlefield confrontation.

quiz.q: What is the refrain that opens and closes the psalm's second half (verses 5 and 11)?

options.text: Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your glory cover all the earth.
options.note: This refrain frames verses 5-11 and expresses a longing beyond personal rescue, for God's glory among all nations.

options.text: In God I trust, I shall not be afraid.
options.note: That refrain belongs to Psalm 56, not this psalm's refrain.

options.text: The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want.
options.note: That refrain belongs to Psalm 23, not Psalm 57.

options.text: Cast your burden upon the Lord.
options.note: That is the key line of Psalm 55, not this psalm's refrain.

quiz.q: How does Jesus' teaching in Matthew 23:37 connect to this psalm?

options.text: Jesus echoes the wing-refuge image, longing to gather Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings.
options.note: This directly parallels David's image of sheltering under God's wings in verse 1.

options.text: Jesus rejects all imagery of refuge and shelter as unspiritual.
options.note: Jesus Himself uses very similar imagery of gathering and sheltering in Matthew 23:37.

options.text: Jesus applies this only to birds, not to people.
options.note: Jesus applies the image of a bird's shelter specifically to His desire to gather and protect people, Jerusalem's children.

options.text: Jesus uses it to condemn David's use of the image.
options.note: Jesus uses the same kind of image approvingly of His own longing to shelter people, not to condemn David's use of it.

questions: David pictures himself sheltering in the shadow of God's wings like a vulnerable bird, even while surrounded by real danger. What would it look like for you to trust God as an intimate refuge, rather than relying on your own strength, in a current difficulty?
David's enemies fell into the very trap they set for him. Where have you seen, in your own life or in Scripture, evil ultimately undoing itself under God's providence?
David moves from anxious plea to a deliberate declaration, my heart is steadfast. What would it mean for you to choose steadfast praise today, even before your circumstances change?

The psalm's refrain longs for God's glory to cover the whole earth, not merely for David's personal safety. How does shifting your prayers from purely personal concerns to God's global glory change the way you pray?

Jesus Himself uses the image of gathering His people under His wings, as David sought shelter under God's. How does knowing Christ personally offers this same refuge change how you come to Him in your fears?

translationNotes.note: Lions is used figuratively for fierce human enemies, a common ancient Near Eastern image for danger and predatory hostility, not a reference to literal wild animals in this context.
Awake, my glory is best understood as David rousing his own inner self, his glory or honor, to praise, rather than referring to an external object; some render it 'awake, my soul.'
This closing section is nearly identical to Psalm 108:1-5, suggesting these verses functioned as an independent unit of praise reused in the compilation of the Psalter.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched via the makor-scripture toolkit for Psalm 57:1-11. No sermon from the trusted cluster (Begg, Keller, Piper, Ferguson, Carson) confirmed for Psalm 57 this session; sermon status set to none.
